projects.summary: Hi HN. I made AJX (Agent Journey Experience). It is a CLI and skill bundle that you run to test what your product feels like to use from the point of view of an agent, and you get back a list of "asks" that would improve your product from an agentic usability perspective: so that agents spend less time, tokens and retries to accomplish tasks with it. How? It works by having an outer loop (AJX harness skill + CLI) that controls an "inner loop": the agent that actually tries out your product. The outer loop investigates the inner loop once it finishes. To try it, copy the prompt from the main page into your favorite agent and it will install the skill and CLI and you can then trigger /ajx skill, give it a prompt and some simple configuration as text, and it helps you with the rest. The outer loop starts loading the configured harness of your choice (claude, codex, kiro-cli etc..) in an environment and configuration of your choice (docker, VM, local, with or without specific skills, specific model, amount of runs, and more), and provides the harness (inner loop) with your input prompt and links, and "definition of done" - what does it mean to succeed with this product? For example with vercel cli you could say "build and deploy a simple hello world with vercel CLI [link]" as the prompt for the AJX test. Once the inner loop harness runs its course, the outer harness loop examines the run, logs and details, and outputs and extract the needed information from that run: retries, tokens, mistakes, assumptions and more, and created a very detailed report, as well as a list of asks that if applied to the product, would improve the agentic journey given the same prompt in the future. I call this "Agent Journey eXperience" it's the agentic equivalent of "User Experience" - if we were to document the journey an agent does when trying your product for the first time in a specific scenario. - Where does it go astray and makes mistakes? - How many retries does it take to succeed with the task? - How much time? - How many tokens? List of ASKS as an output: What features/fixes would the agent want the product to have to save it from making these mistakes or costing extra time and token in the future? here are some examples: - CLI missing a --JSON, which cost lots of parsing of unneeded code - CLI missing commands like doctor, help aliases - DOCS disagree with behavior of the product - Skills pull the agent in the wrong direction - lack of feedback while product is executing - Human friendly CLIs outputs break the agent loop - and much more. Why? I'm a startups solutions architect @ AWS, and previously wrote the art of unit testing and did lots of work on code quality, engineering practiced and continuous delivery) I built AJX (ajx.dev) when I was tasked with giving feedback on an internal upcoming AWS product that is meant to be used by agents. The team wanted feedback from potential users, and I figured that agents are the new potential users. I figured that if I was a product owner, I'd love to know what it feels like to work with my product (CLI, SDK, Website, Docs etc), and that the harder the agents work to use my product, the less people would point their agent at it, or the less the agent would tend to recommend it. Also I think it's useful to have "brag points" that your product is "agent-friendly". I even tested AJX with AJX and it found great of issues with the CLI (for example ajx status was returning the wrong status sometimes, ajx init --task behaved differently than expected, and other cool stuff like that. I envision this being used as part of a CI/CD cycle with a loop until AJX returns "all green" and no ASKS. AJX is still very new - so probably lots of rough edges but in an agent first world, I think it's a step in the right direction: see the world from an agent's POV.

projects.title: Show HN: Jev vs. OpenAI Decision vs. Small Financial World Models: FinBench [video]
projects.author: atul-mehra
projects.summary: Guys - OpenAI Decisions, Jev, World Models are interesting. We ran some tests for the C-suite to decide between OpenAI Decisions vs. their own existing models vs. training their proprietary Financial World Model. Sharing the results of our sample tests. If you like a walkthrough with video of results - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQ We are also trying to reach OpenAI team & community to collaborate on running various tests to help the C-suite to make decisions. Which involves which business cases, they wish to map on which Decision models. Summary: Small Financial World Model compared to OpenAI Decisions. This test is not to build a better model. But to help C-suites make informed choices. There are various considerations viz Latency Cost per decision On-premises or Hosted APIs Regulatory & Compliance Mapping to use cases Financial modelling or LLM-based reasoning as underlying architecture We ran tests to: Predict credit defaults Cross-sell propensity Churn Risk Future cash flows Future state of customers & causal impacts of interventions like no-action, Payment reminders etc. These tests are specific to banking use cases. Why Benchmark & comparison: Small on-prem Decision Models are needed due to latency, cost, regulatory or protecting the proprietary data for Enterprises. This benchmarking helps C-suite executives to decide which option - their in-house models or other options are better. Vaayu FinBench also includes some specific banking-related business cases as examples. World Model also has action-conditioning. Thus, it predicts which decision optimizes the future outcomes. Eg Risk weighted return or prevent default. Core ask from Banks Small Financial World Model is trained on-premesis on proprietary data for enterprises. Scope - This is only for demonstration purposes to give a glimpse of how to compare various options. The dataset & model size is way too small yet. On a larger proprietary dataset, the results need to be benchmarked. Results: Latency - A co-located Small Financial World Model way improves latency. Major part may be coming due to network latency. So this is one area where we would like to discuss alternatives with OpenAI team & community. Is there a smaller on-premesis version for Decision Model avaialble for co-location. Credit Defaults - Our Small Financial World model worked worse than Decision API. Cash Churn & Cross Sell propensity - Our Small Financial World model improved marginally. It’s obvious that since Decision API hasnt seen the propreitary data. The marginal improvement shows model is learning..but our model is very very small (Few 100 thousand parameters) trained on small dataset.. But test demonstrates - architecture is capable of learning better. Action conditions outcomes - This is available in World Model …but we aren’t aware of this in Decision API yet. Financial Modelling - Model is trained finance native can handle temporal & causal scenarios If you like a walkthrough - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQ Disclaimer: This is quick tests results & has some know issues. This is only for demonstration purpose. We have included OpenAI Decisions for now...Including Jev in next releases. At the moment talking to C-suite & Banks for what they wish. We find Decision API & World Models interesting developments especially in finance & enterprises space. Looking forward to collaborate with OpenAI team & community how to enable C-suite to make choices…which are underway right now at enterprises.

projects.title: Show HN: Fermi Poker, a combination of poker betting mechanics with estimation

If you don't want to print out anything, you can also use fermi.org/play to see the questions on your device. Fermi Poker combines the betting mechanics of poker with Fermi estimation questions like "How many new smartphones were sold worldwide in 2024?" or "How many chickens were slaughtered for meat worldwide in 2024?" The aspiration was to create a game that teaches important rationality concepts (Fermi estimation, Bayesian updating, cognitive empathy, world-modeling, emotional regulation, etc.) If you want to host a tournament at your school or university, please consider reaching out as I can provide some funding to cover the cost of poker chips and small prizes.

projects.title: [Dev-circuit-ultra]-自己做的比 OpenSpec 更少上下文、更少流程、更快交付的开发 loop
projects.author: iswalterwu
projects.summary: 这两天优化了自己在用的开发工作流，好处是比 OpenSpec 的上下文维护轻量得多，但不丢框架深度和交付细节。 经过测试，在较短的开发周期下，已经能体现较 OpenSpec 超过 -30% 的 token 成本、-48% 的 cache-read 以及 -51% 的文档维护。仓库里还放了一次单会话的开放任务 A/B，方向和这个一致（模型成本 −29.9%、输入+输出 tokens −36.2%、cache-read −48.6%、留存文档 −51.6%）。 同时，记账与开发完全分离，确保开发过程不会被过期设计或旧想法污染。 [项目地址]( https://github.com/iswalterwu/dev-circuit-ultra) [项目概览]( https://github.com/iswalterwu/dev-circuit-ultra/blob/main/assets/after-setup-en.svg) ## 它是什么 一套面向独立开发者的五步功能开发循环，以 skill 的形式加载到 Claude Code、Codex、pi、DeepSeek Harness 等编码 agent 里： 1. 设计澄清 + 意图卡 2. 单个能独立验收的端到端切片 3. 实现 + 验证 4. 独立审核（普通功能一次；框架级改动加一次结构审） 5. 验收 + 合并 和常见的规格驱动工具不同，它不维护 proposal / tasks / archive，仓库里只保留**现行设计**：设计变了就原地覆盖或删除，功能收尾就删卡。决策历史（包括被否掉的方案）写进项目之外的私有 git 账本；强隔离下，dev 容器没有账本挂载、没有路径、没有凭证，开发 agent 读不到。 这条边界是文件系统级的，不是 prompt 约定。README 里把隔离分成弱 / 中 / 强三档，明确写了只有容器方案才叫"保证"。 ## 最新 A/B：省在哪 同一个 records CLI 开放任务、每个 skill 一个会话、最终交付物盲评： | 相对 OpenSpec | Dev-circuit-ultra | OpenSpec | 差异 | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 模型成本 | $0.0743 | $0.1060 | −29.9% | | 输入 + 输出 tokens | 72,308 | 113,337 | −36.2% | | 缓存读取 tokens | 1,891,968 | 3,678,333 | −48.6% | | assistant 轮次 | 39 | 50 | −22% | | 留存文档 | 2 文件 / 132 行 | 3 文件 / 273 行 | −51.6% | | 盲评总分（30） | 27 | 26 | +1 | 欢迎大家一起探讨，跟大家学习！

projects.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
projects.author: hedgerow-dev

github.name: hedgerow-dev/coldframe
github.description: Low-interaction honeypot for supermarket refrigeration controllers (Danfoss AK-SM 800A, Dixell XWEB 500)

projects.summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io. Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

projects.title: Show HN: A terminal viewer for plain text data files (JSON,YAML,CSV,XML,)
projects.author: rjrodger
projects.summary: When I started working hands-on with OpenAPI specifications, it became clear very quickly that using an editor to read large volumes of deeply nested JSON sucks, a very great deal. So I went looking for something to help, and came across https://jless.io This is an awesome terminal app for navigating nasty JSON documents. I am forever indebted to Paul Martinez for writing this tool. But it did have some gaps. It couldn't reload files that had changed, keeping your place in the JSON structure, which I really needed. And it only loaded one file at a time. But unfortunately it was written in Rust, and I didn't know Rust, and back in the pre-AI days that was kind of a huge blocker. But of course once we got models that could actually write decent code, the obvious idea came to me - I'll just add my features and submit a PR! Happy days. Except by that stage my requirements had grown - I also needed to handle many other file formats, like CSV, TOML, INI, and even XML. So I got side-tracked extending another side-project - an easy going JSON parser that supported comments, and trailing commas, the usual sort of thing. During COVID, with a SaaS startup in the events space now on the rocks, I was looking for some distraction and decided to refactor this little easy-going JSON parser of mine. It used a generated parser and was slow. I read some blog posts about how all production-grade language parsers are pretty much hand-crafted recursive descent, and thought, how hard could it be! Five years later, after many many fun experiments, and production use, I ended up with a runtime parser system: https://tabnas.dev This is a quirky approach to parsing that is partly recursive descent, partly a state machine, and mostly empirical hacking. It works, and it's pretty fast, and I use it for real projects. It has the nice property that grammars are dynamic - you don't generate code, the grammar is executed. A fancy regular expression engine, but revved up to parse anything into a proper abstract syntax tree. Now with that in hand, I could return to the original project and create my own version of jless that solved the itches I needed to scratch: a watch mode; multiple tabs; load any data format into a tree structure Now I still don't know Rust. I mean I like the idea, but there are only so many hours in the day. But now we have AI, so now I do get to go to the candy store. Combining jless.io, and tabnas.dev, and my requirements, I built (caused to be built?), aless - the less for any format! Now this is also a nice stress test for the tabnas parsing engine, and I was very pleased about that too. So if you need to review lots of data structure files on the command line, and need a terminal app to do so, this is for you. I can't help but be struck by the irony however that the need for such a thing is much less now - I mostly get agents to look at large JSON documents now. Still, our puny human brains need help sometimes, and this lets me review documents when I need to. It is also really nice and satisfying to see how easy it is to now bring together open source components to create what is essentially personal software. But I think the key thing out of this little project is that the basic physics of software development remain the same. Software should be built from components glued together. Components should have well-defined interfaces. Aim to reduce cognitive load - this is useful to both humans and machines. Yes, the entire thing could be built from scratch, using a textual specification, and be a mire of over-engineered AI slop, and still be perfectly usable. But the way I actually built it, with AI as a coding companion, using components was deeply satisfying because I still understand the essence of the code, while being able to ignore the accidental complexity. Components give you another layer of abstraction with fewer things to think about, and that allows your human mind to stay in the game.

projects.title: Show HN: GitHub-like reply with "R" for Basecamp and Slack
projects.author: nashbridges
projects.summary: Hello HN! I wrote a browser extension (also available as a userscript) that allows to insert quotes into site's reply message box using selected text + hitting 'r' (as it's done on Github). It targets only specific sites (basecamp.com, slack.com), because that's what we use at our company daily. The idea came out of my boss (who's also a good friend of mine) frustration. He always complained that Basecamp's replies are so inconvenient compared to Github's way. You have to select the quote, copy it into clipboard, then scroll to the reply box, paste it, then select the text again, and finally format it as a quote using editor's toolbar. That's 6 steps vs 2 on Github! Last summer Basecamp rolled out a new facelift featuring a heavy usage of keyboard shortcuts. But "reply with r" was still missing, so another rant from my boss followed :) At that time I was toying with an old browser extension written long time ago as a learning project. I was rewriting it against the new extension API to see what changed/improved. Being immersed into the topic, it was obvious that a thought about "fixing" Basecamp with a browser extension came into my head. So I started working on the Dial R for Reply project during my spare time. I had two clear motivations: 1. I knew it would make someone's life better (myself included). 2. I would learn something new along the way. During the process I realised I could also "fix" Slack replies. It was a bit of trial and error (I didn't use any LLMs for reasons stated above). The hardest part was to dig into each editor's public and private APIs (Basecamp uses lexical, Slack uses Quill). I had to resort to using internals, so be warned -- it might break when site owners decided to update those libraries. On the other hand, hacking a site with an extension is a risky operation anyway (anything may be changed at any time). Key takeaways: 1. browser extensions are cool! Compared to native apps and electron wrappers, you as a customer have such a powerful tool to amend a web application as you like. 2. if you are a library writer, if possible, keep your private state and/or functions accessible to the outside world. Yes, you should clearly mark them as a private, so there's a clear boundary drawn between what can be used safely and what's not. But being able to peek into private state was the only option for me to debug and hack into the application.

projects.title: Show HN: Aggregate Finance, your financial data in a spreadsheet you own
projects.author: mitchthebaker
projects.summary: I started building Aggregate Finance a couple of years ago because I was manually updating a Google Sheet to track my credit card statements, monthly recurring transactions, and spending habits. This seemed perfect for automation as I was having to log in to six separate banking apps to pull this information together. My original intention was to use this tool locally, but I figured it would be an excellent learning opportunity to understand how to scale the application for others to use. The core functionality of Aggregate Finance revolves around syncing banks and brokerages through Plaid to create visuals and data analytics in Google Sheets and OneDrive/Excel, but I've also added Stripe for payments, passkey and TOTP support for MFA (wanted to better learn how WebAuthn works, mostly), and Resend for emailing account updates. The first question you're likely thinking is: isn't this just reinventing the wheel? There's plenty of other personal finance/budgeting apps out there like Rocket Money, Monarch, Copilot Money, YNAB, Tiller, Credit Karma, etc. I personally tried Rocket Money but it left a bad taste in my mouth how my entire financial history was stored on their servers without having direct ownership of the data. Another pain point with these personal finance apps is you're locked into their subscription and lose access to your financial data if you cancel. That's why I opted for the Google Sheet and OneDrive/Excel approach since this persists financial data over time and provides direct data ownership. There's a fair argument that these options still share your financial data with Google or Microsoft, so I built a way to download your financial data locally via CSV/Excel/LibreOffice exports. In terms of data encryption, Aggregate Finance encrypts financial data before it reaches MongoDB: balances, transactions, merchants, statements, holdings, and any user customizations. Each user gets their own AES-256 key rather than a shared key. The reason I went with this approach is for data deletion: when someone deletes their account, their encryption key is deleted as well, so any financial data stored in prior database backups can't be decrypted. I've been using Aggregate Finance with my own live bank accounts and investment holdings, and it's already been helpful. I can see when my credit card statements are due, monitor my entire investment portfolio, keep track of recurring charges, create budgets, and see how my spending pans out over a given month or over the past year. I'm curious whether it's useful for anyone else, and I'd of course welcome any feedback on how I can improve it. You can try it with a free sample spreadsheet that contains a year of example data with no bank connection required at https://app.aggregatefi.com .

projects.title: Show HN: Ferry, a highly customizable and feature-rich file manager for macOS
projects.author: jailbirdBD
projects.summary: I am the main developer of Ferry. The team I am part of began on the demoscene in the mid-90s, but for a long while we are mainly just an indie development studio. Ferry started with me being forced to use macOS at my current workplace, which suddenly replaced a working environment I'd been using during professional career as a programmer: Windows for around 10 years, then Debian/KDE for the last 15 years. Over that time, I'd grown very accustomed to Total Commander on Windows, and later Dolphin on Linux as a file manager, plus a collection of small but very useful tools I'd written for myself on Linux. Moving to macOS was quite an adjustment. I really struggled with Finder and the rather fragmented ecosystem of apps, especially when I couldn't find tools that covered the things I was used to having at my fingertips. Having already written a few internal tools in Swift at work, I started to get familiar with the language while trying out several file managers for macOS without finding one that really suited all of my needs... So one thing led to another, and I eventually decided to build my own version of a better Finder (that's probably how most of the macOS file managers started their journey). Obviously, the first versions were essentially a combination of a slightly improved dual-pane Finder spiced up with basic features from TC, but t'was more than good enough for me. Once I started sharing it with coworkers and friends they began suggesting features I hadn't even considered initially, many of which turned out to be genuinely useful. I know there are quite a lot of file managers out there, so a "what makes Ferry different?" is a totally valid question. Well, Ferry first and foremost tries to be as less opinionated and as much customizable as it's possible, so I have included A LOT of options for personalization. Eg. the layout, the UI, the menus, or the shortcuts are adjustable in many ways, you could even put together something which more or less resembles an old-school Norton Commander-style file manager with a modern toolset if that's your thing. The app also includes a rather big collection of handy tools and tidbits which probably don't seem too interesting up until the point you run into a specific trivial task, and then you realize you have to search and install a tool for it. Main features list: https://ferry.indus3.org/#ftrs Another aspect that's important to me is how the app is made. Having been really involved in the demoscene, I wanted to handcraft as much code as possible and keep AI involvement to a minimum, while still using it to improve quality. Most of Ferry is still written manually, AI mainly helps with the boring parts: proofreading and translations, debugging, tests, temporary tools, code reviews and the site. LLMs have become so advanced that I'm honestly not sure whether this is a good or bad thing for software quality. My skills probably aren't quite on par with a modern LLM agent, but hopefully I can still build something useful and pragmatic by doing most of the work myself. Licensing follows TC's approach: there's a reminder, but you can keep using the app for as long as you like (or until the reminder gets too annoying). Hopefully that's reasonable enough. But if I eventually become really happy with the codebase, I'll most likely release the source code too. At this point, since there are plenty of features, I'm becoming much less interested in adding even more of them and rather focused on getting the existing ones as good as possible: size, stability, performance, memory consumption and above all, bugfixes and code quality. Of course I still listen to users, and if someone suggests a feature which is practical and it improves the UX, I try to include it into a future release. Feel free to contact us, as suggestion and criticism is always welcome!

github.description: An agent paradigm built on an event-driven timeline and a fully plugin-based runtime — it grows and iterates within the environment it runs in.

projects.summary: 我们开源了 Dim，一个以事件时间线为核心的 Agent Harness。 我们希望 Agent 不只是响应一轮轮对话，还能回顾历史、并行探索，并持续推进目标。随着模型越来越聪明，Agent 架构也需要改变：少一些约束，多一些引导，让模型有更大的空间去理解、探索和行动。 主要特点 1. 以事件时间线驱动 Agent 许多 Agent Harness 以消息列表和模型请求为中心，Dim 以一条持续延伸的事件时间线为核心。用户输入、Agent 的判断和行动、工具结果，以及 Harness 自身的工作，都是时间线上的事件。事件写入后不可更改并被分发，负责消费和处理事件的状态机叫 capability。所以 Agent 的历史不只有对话，还有它的观察、行动和结果。 2. 结构化召回历史 内置 recall 工具，Agent 可以结构化地召回整条时间线上的过去对话、事件、行动和结果。用户也可以用 /timeline 跳到任意一条历史消息，再编辑、引用、开分支或 Fork。 3. 通过时间线分支“分神” Dim 支持创建时间线分支（branch 工具），让同一个 Agent 在不同分支里并行探索、反思和推进多条任务线。分支与主分支共享同样的资源和规则。这和 subagent、多 Session 协作不同，是同一个“我”在不同分支里思考和工作。/goal 就是基于分支的目标推进模式。 4. 用插件构造 Agent 的躯体 Dim 基于 rutis 构建多插件体系，会话、模型、工具、权限、审批等能力都是按所有者划分的部件。插件目前可以用 Rust、TypeScript 或 Python 编写。同时支持 MCP、Skills，提供 ACP stdio 网关，也内置 Web 工作区（/web）。 体验 alpha 版 目前提供 alpha 体验版，是单独的 npm 包，命令是 dima： sh npm i -g dimcode-alpha@alpha dima --version dima 支持 macOS / Linux / Windows 的 arm64 和 x64。 首次使用：用 /connect 配置第三方模型的 API Key；如果有 Dim 官方订阅，也可以用 /login 登录使用。 数据放在独立的 ~/.dimcode-alpha，不读写 ~/.dimcode。 默认需要审批工具调用，沙箱为可选开启。 这是预发布版本，接口和行为可能变化。 一起把它做好 Dim 以 MIT 协议开源，欢迎基于它实践自己的想法。上手遇到问题、说明不清楚，或者有想探索的场景，欢迎到仓库 Issues 留下具体反馈。架构文档和 ADR 都在仓库的 docs/ 里，想研究 Agent 运行时设计的可以直接读。

projects.title: Show HN: Penthera, offline pentest security scanner (open-source, rule-based)
projects.author: danosz
projects.summary: local non-AI security for your app/site! For years I had a long .txt file with hundreds of manual security checks I ran before pushing a (client) app/site to live; I am really a rookie compared to the real cyber experts, but just covering the basics has saved us many times from malicious attacks on our infrastructure. With the sprawl of AI generated vibecoded apps (I love it, i think creating should be accessible, but so should be cyber safety) and AI coding tools, our code goes to LLM providers but we'd never know what exactly happens behind the scene, hype harness is just rules imo. As i've started my phd and not building apps (anymore for a living;) I'd decided to open source my rule-based system with some easy onboarding; use it through CLI, NPM, MCP, skill/agent (whatever they might call it in a few years). Its super helpful as a free, open-source alternative to run these checks in your codebase. Having a non-AI solution that costs $0 tokens might not outperform a SOTA security model of a big company; but running internal blue/red hat pentests 24/7/365 should be the norm for a safer internet; having it open-source making it a whitebox system and I hope many people contribute their lists. Its not bulletproof but we score #1 on some public benchmarks among free tools (npm malware, PyPI malware and JS injection bugs) so thats encouraging you can run it pre-commit hook, CI etc - working on a "watch" function that runs it live. Have some flags like --deep for a very intense pentest (SQLi, SSTI, SSRF, XSS, command injection) so be careful and only your own URLs. Also --ai opts-in a local Ollama (or if you want paid also fine) model to find things beyond my rules (the LLM never decides on findings). After you can pass it to you coding agent to fix it; thats up to you. maybe in future ill improve this UX but like to stay local-offline-first anyway feel free to try and give feedback or do a PR if you have some ideas. no signup, $0, local, hackable; read more on the www: penthera.org for some research i've done to make it better/transparent npx penthera --repo . <3 daan

But copying them over, looking them up in a dictionary and making my own flashcards? I was too lazy. So I built a full dictionary into the app, with native speaker pronunciation and verified example sentences from PONS and wiktionary, so you can save a word the moment you don't understand it, or when you're missing one in a conversation. That let me practise situations like sending a package at the post office beforehand. Butt to be honest, it worked in some situations, and in others I failed completely. People speak too fast, use different words, and you can't practise every situation. I really needed to train my general listening comprehension, and YouTube seemed like the best place for that. So I added a YouTube integration: you watch videos, get a comprehension question from time to time, and can add any word to your vocabulary with one click. It's free, with no ads and no premium tier. You can check it out here: https://noentiendo.app I'm happy about any feedback and ideas. Maybe you're learning a language right now and think "it would be cool to practise it that way". Let me know! I've already added German, so if you want a specific language supported, just comment.

projects.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
projects.author: schopra909
projects.summary: My brother and I run a 2-person lab that trains our own generative video models from scratch. The ultimate goal is a set of creative tools that make it easier for anyone to make animation. Video models today are too slow/expensive and lack sufficient controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. In our opinion, they're not usable yet for storytelling. When we set out to build Linum v3 (our next video model) earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools. Typically, you see "latent diffusion models". A VAE (Variational Autoencoder) compresses the input data into a smaller "latent space" and the diffusion model learns how to generate within this subspace. Over the past few months, we've been publishing our work on efficient pixel-space diffusion models. These throw away the VAE, having the diffusion model learn a latent-space optimized for its exact task. This serves 3 purposes: 1) Simplify Architecture (no 2-stage model training) 2) Faster Convergence (11x faster convergence vs. our latent diffusion counterpart) 3) Cheaper Inference (4x more aggressive token reduction in attention context-windows, without significant loss in quality) This past month we were pressure testing our latest architecture (Pyramid-JiT) by training a text-to-image model longer than the typical one-off experiment. Specifically, we trained it for ~$20K on 660M samples. We were surprised by the quality of results, so we thought we'd release it as open weights for the community (Apache 2.0). The research itself is already public, on our website. For us, it's a big stepping stone towards cheaper video models, since pretty much all video models start as image models. We like to say these models have to learn nouns before they learn verbs.

projects.title: Show HN: Cppbolt – A lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust
projects.author: ajtimepyro
projects.summary: Hey HN! I've been working on cppbolt, a lightweight C++ to WebAssembly compiler written in Rust. The idea was to build something that can compile and run C++ directly in the browser without downloading a massive LLVM/Clang toolchain. Unlike projects that bundle LLVM/Clang and can require 100+ MB of compiler assets, cppbolt's compiler payload is around 1 MB. It compiles a supported subset of C++17 directly to standard WebAssembly binaries. Some things it supports: - Classes, inheritance, virtual functions and operator overloading - Templates and a subset of the C++ standard library - Pointers, references, arrays and dynamic memory - Lambdas, structured bindings and range-based loops It comes with a browser playground, CLI and npm package. A few caveats: this is still a work in progress, it doesn't implement the full C++17 standard, and it might not work as expected with certain C++ programs. I'm particularly interested in feedback on the compiler architecture, language support and potential use cases and also interested in connecting with someone who might want to use it in their application. Try it out: - Playground: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/ - Docs: https://ajtimepyro.is-a.dev/cppbolt/book/ - GitHub: https://github.com/AJTimePyro/cppbolt - npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/cppbolt Would love to hear what you think, especially from people who've worked on compilers or WebAssembly.

projects.summary: Hi HN! I made this fun app which combines quite a few ideas, I thought you might like the story: A few months ago I had the idea of looking for anagrams of names. I started with french names using official statistics about first and last names, which also gave me a pretty simple model for likely anagrams: P(first + last) = P(first) * P(last). Then, I started checking which anagra-names (I coined the term) appeared in the 2021 Facebook leak. Finally, I improved my ranking using a factorization model. All this is available as a light and fast webpage thanks to a lot of cool algorithmic tricks detailed here: https://louisabraham.github.io/anagranames/how.html About the use of AI: Claude Code was fantastic for building the frontend (including the interactive globe) and writing the MLX code (I would otherwise have used PyTorch, which is slower on my machine). It also handled the quantization with very little guidance, which was particularly useful since I'm not an expert in that area. That said, I'm glad I learned CS before LLMs existed and still master it enough to work out the ideas and specs for everything else in my head / on paper before handing the implementation over to the agent.

projects.author: Jpoliachik
projects.summary: I made Ramble because I wanted to get off my phone but still be able to capture thoughts, reminders, action items - whatever. Some of my best thoughts happen when I'm playing with my kids or on a run - and this lets me stay in the moment, fire off a quick message on my watch and not get pulled into the screen waiting for AI to respond - never get sucked into 'lets solve this now' mindset. Ramble is designed for Apple Watch & offline first - to capture voice quickly and queue up messages to send when it can. The slim relay backend uses cloud transcription (Grok Whisper currently), then holds the message in an inbox for your agent to pickup and process, then gets purged from the backend after acknowledgement. No accounts, no signups. It uses Apple's App Attest for endpoint security. It works great with current gen personal agents like Muse, GrokBot, etc. (GrokBot supports incoming webhooks so its instant. Muse doesn't, so it polls every couple minutes (without waking the agent)) The linking process is surprisingly easy. Would love to hear what you think!

projects.title: Show HN: Beam – Pairing machines with passkeys; replace SSH&VPN's with Tailcat
projects.author: hermannbjorgvin
projects.summary: A concept I wanted to share that is built on TailScale's Tailcat https://tailscale.com/tailcat The inspiration is that I was thinking of ways to allow my users to be able to pool their machines easily without needing to set up SSH or a VPN. How can you lower the barrier to entry without compromising on security. The end result is you get a remote shell connection and a Tailcat tunnel that only requires your user to know how to use passkeys to verify their machines. Any machine can join the pool without having connected to the others at any point before which is also a strength. The primary weakness is that even though all the passkey assertion and encryption/decryption happens on the browser side you are still trusting a Cloudflare worker to store it. So I think this is more of a solution for things like Herdr, T3 code, etc etc where you want to connect machines in a pool. Each machine also has a small SQLite mail inbox for those purposes, you can queue messages that your machine will receive next time it is reachable. For a more in depth explanation I created this artifact with Fable 5.2 and Astra 6 to clean up the prose: https://claude.ai/artifact/NVHSV1FNmpPaPsqRakskVW

projects.author: raiseCatError
projects.summary: Hey HN and Cats, thank you for checking this out! Github: https://github.com/raiseCatError/meowdisplay EDIT 2: I should've mentioned that MeowDisplay started as a fork of OpenDisplay: https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay which provided the foundational screen capture, virtual display, encoding and iPhone/iPad receivers. I've since taken it in a more phone-first direction, with work on the interaction, streaming and security layers. I've credited OpenDisplay and its developer Philip in the README under "Built on OpenDisplay". MeowDisplay is my take on the control your Mac from your phone scene. Available on iPhones, iPads and Macs, with Android rn in closed testing. The website has interactive illustrative demos if you'd like to see the app demonstrated. I think MeowDisplay does a few things differently, some of which I prefer and you might too. Such as Window view: allowing multiple tabs in split-screen type panes. Traditional Mirror/Extend views exist as alternatives. Floating windows: coming in the 2.1 release. Touch input approaches: Direct Touch(Classic or Natural), experimental Smart Touch, and Trackpad mode alongside Apple Pencil support. Doesn't sacrifice display space for a trackpad, use all of the phone's screen with your preferred mode. Stage Peek: shows a scrollable and searchable list of your Mac's windows on your phone along with an app drawer when you hold and pull on the left edge of your screen. It's free and open source so you can try it and see if it's for you without having to commit to it or anything. EDIT: I've used MeowDisplay during development whilst I was travelling between cities, left my acbook at home clamshell, powered, external display attached, and used it for small tasks remotely, it was pretty reliable even on a 5G network on a moving bus. Meow, Jai

projects.summary: Hi, Dmitri from Radioso here, an open-source platform to design AI agents for customers and visitors in any channel, in the style of Fin/Ada/Decagon. The repo is https://github.com/radioso-ai/radioso and our website is https://radioso.ai Today, your choices are: 1. Buy a very expensive service for your vertical (usually starting with $$ five figures monthly) 2. Get a cheap off-the-shelf chatbot that mostly answers FAQs 3. Build your own, and then also build the inbox, human handoff, audit trail and integrations around it At Radioso we wanted an open-source option that combines the best of all 3. You can integrate it with your own software via API/SDK or your CRM, or run it standalone, either self-hosted or in our cloud. The engine runs multi-step interactions and takes actions: calling your APIs, updating records, booking things. Maybe you’ve tried Parlant; Radioso is the alternative “with batteries included”: RAG, audit trail, customer service inbox, and integrations like Slack and email. Under the hood it’s plain TypeScript + PostgreSQL, works with OpenAI/Anthropic/other models, and is licensed under Apache 2.0 which includes all features (The only thing we keep under EE license is the multi-tenant layer we use to run our own cloud). We have existing customers running it for technical Q&A, course booking, online product recommendations and goods returns, among others, some reaching 92% of conversations automated. We’re currently working on voice support so we can offer a call center. Our ambition is to be “the WordPress of customer-facing AI” :), where people can contribute their favorite plugins and benefit from the ecosystem. Longer term, we think browsing the web will mostly mean talking to your own agent, and when you need a service or a purchase, your agent will talk to the vendor’s agent to get things done. projects.summary: 开源协议：Apache-2.0 ACCP（Agent Collaboration Control Plane）是面向研发团队的自托管 AI 协作管理平台：人在 Web 控制台管任务、项目资料、成果验收和高风险工具审批；Agent 通过本地 Bridge（MCP 工具）、REST 或 Go SDK 接入，领取任务、读取固定上下文快照、汇报进度并提交可核对的成果（含 Git 引用）。每项任务仍由人类负责人接受或退回。它不替代 Cursor / Claude Desktop / Codex 等客户端，也不内置大模型，只做任务 / 上下文 / 验收这一层。 为什么需要它 团队里产品用 GPT、前端用 Cursor、测试用别的客户端时，个人变快了，整体却常卡在对齐：需求散在聊天里、字段名对不上、「完成」标准不一致。ACCP 把协作收成一条可追溯流程：任务有负责人与依赖，资料按版本发布并绑定执行快照，成果经核验后再验收。 主要能力 任务与依赖：指定负责人、执行代理、验收条件；按依赖衔接（例如接口约定发布后再解锁前端接入） 版本化项目资料：需求 / 接口 / 规范按版本发布，Agent 按本次快照读取 Agent 接入：MCP Bridge、REST、Go SDK / CLI；常用工具包括领取任务、读快照与资料、汇报进度、登记成果、查事件等 成果与审批：查看正文与 Git 引用、核验来源；网关内高风险工具操作可走独立人工审批与审计 私有部署：Docker Compose 单机部署；PostgreSQL + NATS JetStream；企业 OIDC 登录 技术栈 Go + React / TypeScript + PostgreSQL + NATS JetStream + OIDC；前端 Vite / HeroUI / Tailwind。本机可用 docker compose 快速起试用环境（仓库 README 有步骤）。 当前状态（诚实说明） 已具备任务、资料、执行、成果、审批与审计的协作闭环，以及团队管理与运维工具，适合受控试用。Claude Desktop 与 Codex 有单人双客户端样例验收记录。正式版本分发、目标规模容量验证和完整恢复验收尚未完成；成果正文当前以文本与 Git 引用为主（正文上限 256 KiB）。欢迎试用与反馈，也欢迎共建。

projects.title: 分享创造 | 因为 Craig Newmark 的一条推文，我复刻了个纯净版克雷格列表（已支持 24 城）
projects.author: no1guangming
projects.summary: 各位 V 友，大家好！ 前段时间在 X 上刷到 Craig Newmark （ Craigslist 创始人）转发的一条推文，极其感慨。 一位工程师问另一位工程师：“如果今天让你重新做一个 Craigslist ，要花多少钱？” 对方的回答直击灵魂：“我们做不出来了。我们已经不知道该怎么把网站做得这么简单了。” 确实，现在的互联网太“重”了。去现在的分类网站（ FB Marketplace 、58 、Carousell ）挂个二手闲置，不仅注册流程繁琐，只要稍微留下点痕迹，马上就会招来铺天盖地的 Bot 爬虫、垃圾短信和钓鱼邮件。虽然 Craigslist 是最早玩“匿名邮件中继”的，但它的技术栈和体验早就停在了上个时代。 为了找回当年那种“纯粹的本地交易”体验，我作为一个独立开发者，决定自己动手写一个精神续作：MingList 。 💡 它长什么样？ 极简、无广告、无弹窗。回归最早的 Web 1.0 逛论坛的感觉，没有任何推荐算法和繁琐的社交绑定。 🛡️ 核心：一套原生的“匿名隐私中继” 为了解决隐私痛点，我重构了中继逻辑。买家想联系你，不需要注册；系统会自动生成一个类似 reply-xxx@minglist.top 的临时中继邮箱。 双方通过这个加密地址双向收发邮件。在你们建立绝对信任之前，你的真实邮箱对全网 100% 隐身。 从根源上切断了爬虫抓取你的真实联系方式的可能。 (坦诚交底：为了防刷和机器人，目前发帖需要一键 Google 登录，但买家浏览和回信是完全免注册的，绝对保护隐私。) 🛠️ 技术架构 & 踩坑 既然要“轻”，那架构就必须极致。 前端/计算：托管在 Cloudflare Pages / Workers 上。 数据/存储：用了 D1 边缘数据库。 发信：Resend 免费版。 成果：直接铺开了美国、英国、加拿大、澳洲、新加坡的 24 个核心城市，而且目前服务器成本几乎为 0 。 🚀 目前的困境与求助 网站刚上线不久，最核心的邮件中继送达率我已经反复测试跑通了。但现在遇到了所有双边市场最痛的“冷启动”问题——很多城市的列表还是空的，用户来了又走。 传送门： https://minglist.top 灵感出处： https://x.com/craignewmark/status/2107052870163952117 想请教 V 站的各位大神，给点硬核的建议： 架构拓展：这种纯 Cloudflare 的边缘 Serverless 方案，如果真遇到恶意刷接口或大批量并发，D1 数据库大概在什么量级会遇到瓶颈？我该提前做哪些限流预案？ 极客冷启动：在没有一分钱推广预算的情况下，除了去 Reddit 的相关板块硬发帖，还有哪些“野路子”可以快速搞到第一批真实的种子用户？ 产品吐槽：欢迎直接点进网站疯狂拍砖，说它太简陋也没关系！ 感谢各位！

projects.title: Show HN: Airlock – Policy-as-code for fleets of AI coding agents
projects.author: lovetocode
projects.summary: My name is Matt and I am building Airlock. Airlock is going to be an open standard on managing autonomous fleets of engineering agents. I am seeking constructive feedback on the direction of this project and also asking what are your major pain points with managing AI use at larger businesses. Right now I am running my own company using this framework with a total of 23 workflows across four large scale projects. Airlock is still really early, only 3-4 weeks old. Airlock's configuration standard is aimed to be open source and I will also open source the backplane once I gain a bit more confidence in what I have built here and it is a bit more ready for public scrutiny. Today the schema itself and the reusable GitHub actions are publicly available. I will selfishly figure out how to monetize this at some point but my desired customer is going to be larger enterprises. Airlock kind of does a lot of things but if I had to sum it up in several bullet points it would be: 1) Allows for the configuration of agent behaviors and life cycles under version control. Each agent run proves who it is with GitHub’s OIDC token, and Airlock trades that for a GitHub token that lasts one hour and can only touch the repos and permissions listed in that agent’s role file. 2) Allows for configuring levels of autonomy starting with a repository's base autonomy level with stricter overrides down to individual files within a code base. (e.g. you trust agents for most of the repo but perhaps you want extra gating around the 'billing' or 'auth' modules). 3) Supports a standard autonomy scale. At level 4 agents are leading a project's direction while at level 1 they are dependent on humans to lead the direction of a project. 4) Provides an out-of-the-box OTEL collector that stores a subset of agent actions you would care about in the event of an audit. I’m exploring storing agent prompts and user prompts so that only the customer can decrypt them, and haven’t decided how. 5) Comes with a shadow mode that allows you to run Airlock and observe how it would behave in your org without turning it on. To try it you just need to install the GitHub App, create a policy repository and run on GitHub hosted runners. I personally use self-hosted runners on EC2 spot instances. Visit https://airlock.lunareng.com/docs/quickstart to get started. I have been really passionate lately about exploring how businesses of the [near] future will effectively manage autonomous development using agents at scale. I want to help answer the question of how can the business better manage AI spend, prioritization of token usage, auditability of agent actions and compliance with various governance, risk and compliance frameworks. I am coming from the perspective of being an engineer for 15+ years but I have somehow managed to also develop a good understanding of how larger businesses operate. My vision of the future looks like a world where engineers don't use agent harnesses directly from their computer [for coding]. Instead engineering teams are managing a larger backlog of work that is automatically picked up by these agents. Engineering will instead be less about writing code and more about effectively deploying technology to solve business problems. Thanks for taking a look and I look forward to meeting you in the comments. References: https://github.com/lunareng/airlock-actions https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/role.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/autonomy.schema.json https://airlock.lunareng.com/schema/config.schema.json https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-dev... https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutori...

projects.title: Show HN: Sentient, Your Coding Agent Shouldn't Be a Black Box
projects.author: epynonymous
projects.summary: after working quite rigorously for a few months with claude code, I found out that I was blindly approving permission requests for the sake of progressing my projects, this led me to realize that coding agents generate hundreds of commands underneath the covers which is necessary, but quite scary if you ask me. you've probably seen news recently about agents deleting databases or environments in production by accident. so i wanted to create something to gain visibility into what's actually happening and potentially block things before they occur. coding agents often log everything that they're doing, but even still, i want the ground level truth of what's happening. that's why i created sentient, written using claude code. it's open source (mit license), runs completely locally, no cloud syncing, read only, and watches actions straight from the kernel. all of this is summarized with a hopefully simple web ui. i run claude code on linux, so kernel tracking relies on tetragon, but, at the same time, i am trying to get approval to use security endpoint on mac, and will eventually roll out on windows. if you want to run sentient today against just the agent logs without kernel logs, that's also available now, you just need golang and sqlite3 to build. and today, i'm only supporting claude code, but will eventually get to codex and the like. please have a try, ping me if you have any questions or comments: hello@nosaka.ai https://github.com/nosaka4i/sentient https://nosaka.ai/blog/sentient

projects.title: Show HN: Solous, a journaling app like a social media for emotions inside of you
projects.author: solous
projects.summary: Solous is a private journaling app. This app is inspired by movies like inside out or Yumi's Cells where we all have emotions inside us. When we write it is one of our emotions writing it. We want to talk to ourselves between these debating ideas and emotions. We are solo but also there are persons inside us. That's where the name is from solo-us. In Solous, you can reply to your own message anytime. It supports normal stuff like tag and search. I try to make it as secure as possible with e2ee as an option. I am the sole builder of the app. I built this app mostly for myself in my free time with Claude. Yes I vibed 100% but I am familiar with aws and python, I am a decent programmer. It is true that these days, everyone can do that. But it still takes time and effort to make it run smoothly and polish features and make it easy to use. I don't believe the future of software is everyone vibe their own stuff. The most efficient way is still to use several good apps. I think there may be more diversity instead of everyone use app store or play store. Because it is made for myself, it has no reminder emails, sometimes, I even don't journal for days, but I feel good when I write one. I think it is good to record what happened in life. Especially when I feel bad. And it is private, it has two factor login, security keys such as face id or whatever you use to unlock your phone, and it has optional end to end encryption. At first I want to make it default, but then I realized it takes some time to setup and maybe it will reduce conversion. so I leave it for whoever care about privacy. The app is free for now. For free tier, there is 1GB limit on uploads and how many journaling you can do (if you write on your own not using ai, you will be ok with free tier). Later I will charge money if you need more space and maybe if you want to give me more money, you can become member and maybe I will open some private features for members or provide more customization options. That's the idea. I will be around today, please try and let me know. Thank you!

projects.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
projects.author: hedgerow-dev

github.name: hedgerow-dev/coldframe
github.description: Low-interaction honeypot for supermarket refrigeration controllers (Danfoss AK-SM 800A, Dixell XWEB 500)

projects.summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real. Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io. Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

projects.title: Show HN: Repairer – close the breach when a Linux flaw goes public
projects.author: jaekwon
projects.summary: As we've seen with the Ubuntu critical CVE-2026-98432 (CVSS 9.8), AI-dicovered zero day exploit are being reported at an exponential rate and we don't have the process for dealing with the flood of exploits in real time. What we need is an AI-based system for autopatching systems based on real time information. The vendor's fix can take days or weeks to be out (is the Ubuntu thing patched yet?) and meanwhile the grid is vulnerable to exploitation, especially AI worms. Repairer is a small program that runs on each of your servers. The day an exploit goes public it puts up a stopgap that blocks it, and once the real fix is up it takes the stopgap back off by itself. A stopgap only takes something away — drop certain packets, turn off a kernel module or service, remove a setuid bit. It never opens a port, installs or downloads anything, nor runs code. It arms an undo playbook before applying the stopgap, so the change reverts if affects any services. It only ever acts on rules you sign with a (hardware) crypto wallet. Let's go further: stopgaps are written and checked by a swarm of AI agents (gnosh.ai sessions) running on gno.land, each with bonded stake. Each stopgap is run on fresh machines, and whoever is caught lying loses their stake to whoever caught them. The agent is built and tested on Ubuntu and Debian, all open source, standard-library Go. More distros coming. Let's build repairer together. https://gno.security/repairer/ https://github.com/gnosecurity/repairer

projects.title: Show HN: Agentic Identity Broker, OAuth Delegation for AI Agents
projects.author: jbspeakr

github.name: zalando-incubator/agentic-identity-broker
github.description: Identity broker for AI agents with OAuth2 delegation and consent management

projects.summary: Hi HN, I’m Jan. I am co-author of the Agentic Identity Broker (AIB), an MIT-licensed OAuth2 broker in the Zalando Incubator, that lets a user give an AI agent scoped, revocable access to MCP services. The broker solves three major challenges that are especially relevant in corporate environments: (A) Enable users to delegate workloads to agents without providing the agents all the user’s tokens. (B) Connect fragmented identity and authorization systems. (C) Centralize tool approvals and audit logging. We built AIB to fill an infrastructure gap in our own agent platform. At this moment in time, IETF working groups are still finalizing standards for agent identity, and vendors are still turning the necessary infrastructure into off-the-shelf products. We needed that infrastructure today. How it works: the user consents once per agent and service. The broker stores the third-party tokens encrypted. At request time a gateway (e.g. Agentgateway) does RFC 8693 token exchange. Agents never see user tokens and MCP servers only implement tools and don’t need to care about all the OAuth 2.1 plumbing. AIB is v0.1 and runs in production, bringing together hundreds of our agents with dozens of internal and external MCP servers. To try it locally: clone the repo, run "just compose-up-detached". The current features focus on on-behalf-of (OBO) use cases, where human actors delegate to agents. Next we are looking to also support headless agents, where agents are invoked by machines. Intent-based authorization is yet another package on our roadmap. If you’ve built either, or have feedback on the UI/UX, I’d like to hear from you!

projects.title: Show HN: Penthera, offline pentest security scanner (open-source, rule-based)
projects.author: danosz
projects.summary: local non-AI security for your app/site! For years I had a long .txt file with hundreds of manual security checks I ran before pushing a (client) app/site to live; I am really a rookie compared to the real cyber experts, but just covering the basics has saved us many times from malicious attacks on our infrastructure. With the sprawl of AI generated vibecoded apps (I love it, i think creating should be accessible, but so should be cyber safety) and AI coding tools, our code goes to LLM providers but we'd never know what exactly happens behind the scene, hype harness is just rules imo. As i've started my phd and not building apps (anymore for a living;) I'd decided to open source my rule-based system with some easy onboarding; use it through CLI, NPM, MCP, skill/agent (whatever they might call it in a few years). Its super helpful as a free, open-source alternative to run these checks in your codebase. Having a non-AI solution that costs $0 tokens might not outperform a SOTA security model of a big company; but running internal blue/red hat pentests 24/7/365 should be the norm for a safer internet; having it open-source making it a whitebox system and I hope many people contribute their lists. Its not bulletproof but we score #1 on some public benchmarks among free tools (npm malware, PyPI malware and JS injection bugs) so thats encouraging you can run it pre-commit hook, CI etc - working on a "watch" function that runs it live. Have some flags like --deep for a very intense pentest (SQLi, SSTI, SSRF, XSS, command injection) so be careful and only your own URLs. Also --ai opts-in a local Ollama (or if you want paid also fine) model to find things beyond my rules (the LLM never decides on findings). After you can pass it to you coding agent to fix it; thats up to you. maybe in future ill improve this UX but like to stay local-offline-first anyway feel free to try and give feedback or do a PR if you have some ideas. no signup, $0, local, hackable; read more on the www: penthera.org for some research i've done to make it better/transparent npx penthera --repo . <3 daan

projects.title: Show HN: Securing GrokBot
projects.author: maximelb
projects.summary: A friend at another tech startup was telling me how they started using Grok Bot and loved it. Surprise surprise they also got pretty worried about what it's doing and the visibility they had. Digging under the hood, hey there's a Linux VM and a Chrome browser. This is really cool because it essentially defines an environment that is really similar to a typical workstation. After some playing around I got the LimaCharlie EDR installed, the Chrome LC EDR installed and the email provider connected to the LC Email Security. Took a few iteration to make it all smooth but it works great on the free community edition! So you get to see what is executing on the box, where the bot is browsing and emails in and out. I built a couple detections using AI and just made it a doc in our documentation so you can just tell Grok Bot: """ Secure my Grok Bot with LimaCharlie by following https://docs.limacharlie.io/grok-bot/ """ The TL;DR; of what it does: - all of it goes to your own private tenant - installs a linux EDR on the box - installs a Chrome extension that is essentially an EDR in your browser - if you want, connects your gmail (any IMAP is supported really) and is like an EDR for the email - If you want it sends the alerts to your Grok Bot (I'm curious to see the advantage of a feedback loop here), or it's available on the web app.limacharlie.io The other option I left in was to leave the CLI authenticated on the Grok Bot. The interesting bit about that is that because the CLI has 100% coverage of the platform, you can ask the Grok Bot to start setting up new alerts, investigate alerts, configure everything... I tried to make it more generic for other AI agents where I have no idea what the environment is: https://docs.limacharlie.io/2-sensors-deployment/tutorials/s... though disclaimer I have not tried it yet, but it's not rocket science and more frontier AI models are now rocket scientists. The advantage that Grok Bot has is that it fundamentally allows things to execute on the VM and talk out. The other ones (Muse, Dots) seem to proxy every single thing and generally be extremely difficult to extend. Anyway, hope it helps some of you! (and yes, got it to make a cool video :D) https://youtu.be/yZZuBgKWd1k

github.name: cattlecloud/litesql
github.description: litesql is a Go library for convenient, easy, and performant use of SQLite3 databases in Go programs

projects.summary: Using SQLite in Go is deceptively easy. If you just import the popular github.com/mattn/go-sqlite3 as the database/sql driver implementation and start making queries, things will work great until you start hitting SQLITE_BUSY errors as traffic increases. Then you go down the same path of many gophers before you, finding GitHub and forum posts providing conflicting information on best practices for pragma values and connection handling. So I created https://github.com/cattlecloud/litesql Which provides a nice abstraction, making it easy to accidentally do the right things when using SQLite in your Go program. In particular it pools connections for read transactions and isolates a dedicated write connection for writes. It also sets pragma values to much more reasonable defaults, like isolation levels, foreign keys, cache sizes, etc. On top it provides a nice abstraction for creating periodic snapshots with retention policies. There is also litesqltest for one-line test database creation in unit tests. Hopefully you or your agents might find it useful.

projects.author: DearFox
projects.summary: 想起什么说什么,基本是要做微信小游戏就需要了解的. iOS 上微信小游戏能用的内存有上限：整个微信进程内存和显存共用大约 1G 到 1.4G(具体看手机内存)，超过就会被系统杀掉；另外 5 秒内收到两次内存警告，微信也会直接销毁小游戏。 别以为你游戏资源包只有几百 MB 就没事。PNG 、JPG 只是文件小，进显存要解开成原始像素，每个像素 4 字节，小游戏占用只看分辨率：一张 2048×2048 的图不管文件多小，都占 16MB ，开了 mipmap 还要再多约 1/3 。要是你的游戏资源几百 M,基本玩着玩着就必崩溃. 解决办法是用 ASTC 压缩纹理：显卡能直接读压缩后的数据，4×4 块的显存是原来的 1/4 ，6×6 约 1/9 ，代价是画质略有损失(我自己测试看不出分别)；再配合用完及时卸载资源，就能把峰值压下来。拿我游戏来说，战斗峰值从约 1G 降到了 200MB. ASTC 压缩还有个问题,可能会把某个类型的图片变成洋红色,真机才会出现,所以一定要测试好. 用户手机发热可以在小游戏网页后台给你的游戏接入高性能模式,能大幅度降低发热问题,其他也有能优化的,腾讯这点好在每个文档里面都有一键复制,直接给你的 AI 看,完美接入. 网页后台显示 100 用户就可以开启流量主,手机看要 1000,这里以网页后台为主. 任何游戏,一定要弄新手教程,用户进来几秒不知道干啥,绝对就退了,想象你自己玩小游戏,有那么耐心吗? 游戏版本审核的时候,只要你的资源需要额外下载,审核界面一定要选择联网,而不是单机,这里不是看你游戏的类型,只要有云上资源,就要联网,不然审核员用不能联网的环境审核失败,会直接打回. 加载云上资源的时候,游戏一定要显示具体的大小或者文件进度,我买的腾讯 cdn,按理来说网络肯定可以,但是几次遇到下不动的情况,如果你的游戏没有详细说明,用户可能会以为卡死,直接就退了. 第一次版本审核成功,后台会建议你用他们的代码加固插件,用的时候代码混淆选中等就行,高选项会直接让主包大于 4M. 接入好友排行功能,要在后台开启这个功能,不然游戏不保报错,但是也不显示内容,会让用户疑惑. 每个游戏可以开启新游种子,基本会给量让你开启流量主,一定要把版本弄好再开启,不像我,新手引导都没有就开启了,浪费了... 就说这么多吧,哎,不做游戏看别的游戏都是垃圾,一做才发现真的难啊,总是有一些问题出现,更难受的是辛辛苦苦做完,没有流量 现在小游戏不花钱推,基本都没入尘烟了 我的游戏是割草类游戏,就是各种技能搭配,纯爽游,感兴趣的朋友微信搜:站桩修仙

projects.title: Show HN: Pots – Open-source Grok Bot alternative, used by 6 startups for a month
projects.author: Crokily
projects.summary: Hi HN, I'm Crokily. Pots is an AI coworker that lives in the chat your team already uses: Slack, Discord, Telegram, or any channel with a Chat SDK adapter. It is MIT-licensed and runs on a machine you give it, with the model you choose. To be honest, the first time I used Grok Bot, its design really impressed me. Unlike OpenClaw before it, it was not just Claude Code connected to a chat app. It truly cared about how it works with people. It felt like a living AI assistant, and working with it was painless. That is the idea I kept learning from the whole time I built Pots: it is not an agent hooked up to a chat channel. It should be a coworker that feels alive and is comfortable to work with. But Grok Bot is only Grok's bot. Which model you get depends on your X subscription, your data and your machine are all in the cloud, and most of all, it is a standalone app, and most of its features serve that app. Pots is a bit different. In Sydney I have talked with quite a few founders. Grok Bot is good, and it helps them a lot with their personal tasks. But when I asked who had actually put Grok Bot into their company's work to make their startup team faster, nobody had. So I think Pots is in a different place from Grok Bot, and from most open-source Grok Bot alternatives: it grew out of what real startup teams need. Before I open-sourced it, 6 small startups I met at startup events had been using it with me for over a month. Pots is built first for the channels startup teams already work in, not for an app of its own, so most of what it does serves the places where you actually work. The teams use Pots as a middle layer: a CEO talks ideas through with the team in chat, Pots listens, and then it builds a prototype that both sides can check. They use Pots for competitor research: because Pots runs inside their channels, it knows their product well. Not only the GitHub repo, but the team's daily discussions and what the team cares about. Pots has been listening quietly the whole time, so it knows the product with no setup at all. It also works well with each channel: it talks to people with the channel's own controls, like Slack and Discord buttons and cards, and when it hands over something complex, it deploys a page with its built-in server so everyone sees it in a better form. So Pots is different from Grok Bot and from most open-source alternatives. It came out of what real startup teams need. Its channel features start from what each company's work needs, and it can join your real work setup with no setup and still do well, instead of being one more app that nobody uses and that is hard to start with. And it ran in real business for a while before I cleaned it up and open-sourced it. The difference from Grok Bot is also exactly why I made Pots an open-source Grok Bot alternative. I have OpenAI and Claude subscriptions with plenty of quota, and my own servers, so I don't want an X subscription to limit me. I want to use whatever model I want and do whatever I want. I can even switch to an open model, and none of my data goes into anyone's pocket. Try it (Node 24+, macOS, Linux or Windows): the easiest way is to ask your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) to read docs/for-agents.md in the repo and set up Pots for you. Or by hand: npm install -g pi-durable-bot, then pots init. I'd love feedback, especially on how it decides when to act.

projects.title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
projects.author: apiclay
projects.summary: Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy. Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist. ApiClay makes that whole loop easier. You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live. But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace. If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links. You can also turn what you already have into an API: * MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints. * Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API. * Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing. * Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products. For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data. There are also practical data tools beyond discovery: * Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result. * Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes. * Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs. * Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper. For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use. *ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.* We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

projects.title: [开源] 写了个 Antigravity 进程级代理补丁（附 IDE 插件），不挂 TUN、不动内网路由~
projects.author: yuaotian
projects.summary: # 又又造了个轮子：不挂 TUN 、不动内网路由，让 Antigravity 独立走代理的免驱动补丁 用 Antigravity 时，遇到过系统代理已经开了，部分请求还是连不上的情况。开 TUN 能解决一些问题，但我只是想让 Antigravity 走代理，不想为了它再调整其他软件的网络规则。 所以写了个 Antigravity Proxy：给 Antigravity 单独指定代理，不用开 TUN ，也不修改系统代理设置。 项目地址：[GitHub · antigravity-proxy]( https://github.com/yuaotian/antigravity-proxy)，BSD-2-Clause 开源。 ## 能做什么 目前支持 Windows 下的 Antigravity IDE 、桌面版和 CLI ，提供 x86 / x64 版本。支持 SOCKS5 和 HTTP 代理，也支持账号密码认证。 使用前需要自己准备好可用的代理。比如已经在用 Clash ，就填它的本地代理地址和端口，继续用原来的节点。 IDE 版还配了一个插件，日常操作可以直接在界面里完成： - 修改代理地址、端口，测试连接； - 查看代理状态、实时日志和出口 IP ； - 检测 Gemini 可达性，辅助排查连接问题。 另外处理了一个比较麻烦的情况：Antigravity 更新后，安装目录里的补丁可能被清掉。IDE 插件会在下次启动时检查并补回，按提示重启即可，不用再手动复制。 ## 怎么安装 **IDE 用户**可以直接在扩展市场搜索 `Antigravity Proxy`，或从 [Open VSX]( https://open-vsx.org/extension/yuaotian/antigravity-proxy) 安装，按提示配置代理并重启。 **桌面版和 CLI 用户**可以使用仓库里的在线安装脚本，也可以从 [Releases]( https://github.com/yuaotian/antigravity-proxy/releases) 下载对应的发布包。具体步骤放在 README 里，帖子就不贴长命令了。 ## 原理和适用范围 底层是放在应用目录里的 `version.dll`，通过 Hook 网络连接，让 Antigravity 相关进程使用配置好的代理。不装虚拟网卡，也不接管整台电脑的流量。 有两个使用边界提前说一下： - 补丁作用于 Windows 进程，WSL 内的程序需要单独配置代理。 - 代理连通不等于服务端一定接受请求。遇到 `User location is not supported`，还需要排查出口地区和服务端限制，安装补丁并不保证解决这类报错。（ PS：换其他国家 IP ，比如新加坡、日本、美国等） 如果你也只是想让 Antigravity 单独走代理，可以试试。遇到问题欢迎提 Issue ，附上应用版本和脱敏日志，方便定位；有改进想法也欢迎交流或提 PR 。

projects.title: Show HN: Usul – Express neural networks as raw math in C++23
projects.author: ronny2fresh
projects.summary:
SO, Usul-cpp is a library I've written in C++, it is based around allowing data scientists to create their models without heavy libraries such as tensorflow, and just express their models using maths, and Usul will handle the rest. There is builtin tensor support, auto-grad, back-prop and its quite fast. I wrote it because, it seemed less mystifying to read maths instead of a random class that supposedly does something. I wrote it from scratch in cpp (23) due to the fact that I wanted to emphasise on precision, however it's subtly built on top of xtensor. check it out in action #include <usul.hpp> using namespace std; int main() { double LR = 0.1; int EPOCH = 5000; // lets write the forward pass Tensor X = { {0.0, 0.0}, // this is what we're feeding it {0.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 0.0}, {1.0, 1.0}, }; // this is what we're after Tensor Y_true = { 0.0, // xor{0.0, 0.0} = 0.0 1.0, // xor{0.0, 1.0} = 1.0 1.0, // xor{1.0, 0.0} = 1.0 0.0 // xor{1.0, 1.0} = 0.0 }; Y_true.reshape({4, 1}); // we are now going to create a single layer, double neuron network // each layer will have a bias and weights tensor. auto W1 = generate_random_matrix({2, 4}, -1.0, 1.0); auto B1 = generate_random_matrix({1, 4}, -1.0, 1.0); auto W2 = generate_random_matrix({4, 1}, -1.0, 1.0); auto B2 = generate_random_matrix({1, 1}, -1.0, 1.0); // this is the training loop for (int i = 0; i < EPOCH; i++) { // so lets do one forward pass // first layer auto Z1 = X % W1 + B1; auto A = Z1.ReLU(); // second layer auto Z2 = A % W2 + B2; // activation // should be - auto S = Z2.activate(Activate::Sigmoid); auto S = Z2.Sigmoid(); // Loss // should be - auto Loss = S.loss(Loss::MSE); auto loss = (S - Y_true) * (S - Y_true); loss = loss.mean(); cout << "Loss: " << loss << "
"; cout << "guesses: " << "
" << S << "
"; cout << "should be: " << Y_true << "
"; loss.backwards(); W1.step(LR); B1.step(LR); W2.step(LR); B2.step(LR); } } which will output Guesses: Tensor({{ 0.027546}, { 0.963592}, { 0.964138}, { 0.038964}}, shape=(4,1)) should be: Tensor({{ 0.}, { 1.}, { 1.}, { 0.}}, shape=(4,1)) Loss: Tensor( 0.001222, shape=()) Just write the maths, and Usul-cpp will handle the rest, it is extremely lightweight, and the entire library is memory safe. And its called Usul, because I'm a huge dune fan. You can view the project at [ https://github.com/crushr3sist/Usul-cpp ]( https://github.com/crushr3sist/Usul-cpp ) Any ideas for what to do next are all welcome, you can also pull and implement features that you think could improve this project. (no vibecoded prs please, this project is not vibe-coded)

projects.title: Show HN: QueenMQ – slow LLM calls blocked our Kafka partitions, so we built it
projects.author: aliceviola
projects.summary: Hi HN, I'm Alice. Over the last year, at Smartness, the company where I work, we built a new message broker, open source under Apache 2.0. During this year it has replaced Kafka almost completely for us. I would like to show it to you and try to explain what is different about it. First, long story short: in 2025 we launched a new product in our suite. Like all the others it used Kafka for messaging, and like many other companies we were using Kafka as a message queue, wrongly and knowingly. In this product head-of-line blocking hurt a lot: an LLM call takes seconds to minutes, and it blocked every other chat in the same partition. We first built a hack: we saved the Kafka messages in Postgres, ordered by the entity we needed (a chat_id, for example), processed them, and sent them back to Kafka. Then we decided to build a real broker on that idea. It took a year, from C++ plus Postgres to, today, a single Rust binary with data replicated on disk by Raft. I designed this system, so I am biased. Still, I believe QueenMQ holds a new paradigm that turns a message broker into something more powerful, while staying simple. What QueenMQ is, compared to what you already know: Like Kafka, it has partitions, but in QueenMQ they are dynamic (not preallocated) and you can use a lot of them (tested up to 10 million). Like Kafka it is a log, but there is one Raft leader per tenant, so all of a tenant's writes go through one node, which allows transactions without 2PC. Head-of-line blocking can only happen inside one partition, which is one business entity, like a customer or a chat. If you need a plain queue, you can use a different partition for every message. Like RabbitMQ, it has ACK, NACK, retries and a DLQ: this makes it a message queue. It has no routing on push and no exchanges, though. Like a database: thanks to its etcd-like design, it runs transactions that include ACKs, pushes to other queues, KV writes and timers, and it has atomic locks. The KV store is replicated by Raft and keeps the application's state. It is linearizable. It also has strong streaming features: the SDKs can receive one single log with all the messages of all the queues, with one clock and one order. On top of it there are the classic streaming features, like windows, and some less common ones. Clients talk to it over HTTP (the clients are thin, the intelligence is in the broker), and it is Kafka-compatible (although that way you cannot use all of its strengths). The idea underneath is the change from seeing a message broker as a pure "handler" of messages to one where you can offload a lot of application logic that you would otherwise write yourself. In our company it let us remove outbox tables, cron jobs and many other things. On three beefy machines (24 vCPU, NVMe, 88 GB of RAM), QueenMQ sustains 3M msg/s of 256-byte messages, up to 10M partitions, with p99 latency around 20 ms and every write fsynced on two nodes. Of course, with a single leader per tenant, it does not scale by adding more machines. We tested it hard: 226 tests of our own, written with the Jepsen library, on up to 5 nodes. It is changing the way we design the systems and products of our company. I believe in this project and I believe in open source, and I am really glad that Smartness thinks the same way. It is hard to find the time and the money to build something like this without a company behind you. I would love to get questions, the harsh ones too (like how many times this thing crashed production), and feedback. docker run -p 6632:6632 ghcr.io/queen-mq/queen:2.8.0
